findings.title: Validator calls BlockedEmail.should_block?, which writes to the DB, so stats are counted more than once per signup
findings.body: `should_block?` increments `match_count`, sets `last_match_at` and saves the record. It is called from inside a validator, which should be side-effect free. `UsersController#create` calls `user.valid?` and then `user.save`, which validates again, so one signup attempt bumps the counters at least twice. Any other `valid?` call on a user with a changed email does the same. Statistics for `do_nothing` entries are inflated. Entries for `block` can be written outside the save transaction, so they are not rolled back. The lookup-and-record-hit logic should run once at a deliberate point, or the validator should do a read-only check.

findings.title: Non-atomic read-modify-write on match_count loses updates under concurrency
findings.body: `record.match_count += 1; record.save` loads the row, increments in Ruby and writes back the absolute value. Two concurrent signups with the same email both read N and both write N+1, so a hit is lost. It also runs a full save with callbacks and a uniqueness validation query on every check. Use `BlockedEmail.increment_counter(:match_count, record.id)` or `update_all(['match_count = match_count + 1, last_match_at = ?', Time.zone.now])` so the increment happens atomically in SQL.

findings.title: Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive and not normalized, so it is trivially bypassed
findings.body: `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` is an exact string match, and the unique index on `blocked_emails.email` is case-sensitive too. If `bad@spamclub.com` is blocked, `Bad@SpamClub.com` or ` bad@spamclub.com` passes the check. The rest of the codebase normalizes emails with `Email.downcase` and `strip`. Stored and queried emails should be normalized (for example downcased on save and on lookup), otherwise the blocking feature is easy to evade.

findings.title: Array literal on the controller prototype is shared across instances
findings.body: `rejectedEmails: Em.A([])` is declared in `extend({...})`, so the one array lives on the prototype and is shared by every instance. `pushObject` then mutates shared state, so rejected emails persist across all controller instances (and across tests). It should be initialized per instance in `init`, for example `this.set('rejectedEmails', Em.A([]))`.

findings.title: Invalid computed-property dependent key 'rejectedEmails.@each'
findings.body: In Ember, `@each` must be followed by a property name (`rejectedEmails.@each.foo`). To observe array membership changes the key should be `rejectedEmails.[]`. With a bare `.@each` the `emailValidation` property may not be invalidated when `pushObject` adds a rejected email. The "rejected email" feedback then wouldn't update until `accountEmail` changes.

findings.title: Client marks any email-error rejection as 'invalid' and hides the real server reason
findings.body: The JS adds the email to `rejectedEmails` whenever `errors.email` is present, and `emailValidation` then shows the generic `user.email.invalid` text. The server-side reasons (`blocked`, `not_allowed`, already taken) are not shown in the field. The new `user.email.blocked` message appears only in the flash, and the inline field gives a misleading "invalid" message. The per-field error from `errors.email` should be used as the validation reason.

findings.title: Tests don't cover validator interaction with whitelist/blacklist or the User model integration
findings.body: The spec only stubs `BlockedEmail.should_block?` and checks the error toggles. It does not cover the moved whitelist/blacklist logic, the short-circuit when an earlier error exists, a nil or blank value, or an end-to-end `User` validation. It also does not cover the new `errors`/`values` JSON returned by `UsersController#create`, or the repeated validation calls that inflate `match_count`. Regressions in the refactor out of `User#email_validator` would not be caught here.
